title: Reconnecting With Yourself After Years of Putting Others First
excerpt: When you've spent years meeting everyone else's needs, finding your way back to your own can feel unfamiliar — here's a gentle place to start.

body.text: There is a particular kind of tiredness that comes from being endlessly available. You are the reliable one, the one who remembers, who smooths things over, who says yes. From the outside it can look like generosity, and often it is. But somewhere in the middle of meeting everyone else's needs, a quiet question can begin to surface: what do I actually want? And with it, sometimes, an uncomfortable blankness where the answer should be.

If you have spent years putting others first, reconnecting with yourself can feel strangely unfamiliar — even a little disloyal. This is not because something is wrong with you. It is because attention, like a muscle, grows strong in the direction you use it. Turned outward for long enough, it can take practice to turn some of it back toward yourself. This piece is a gentle place to begin.

Most people who put others first did not choose it as a strategy. It was learned — often early, often for good reasons. Perhaps being attuned to others' moods kept things calm at home. Perhaps your needs felt like too much, so you learned to make them small. Perhaps being helpful was how you felt safe, valued, or loved. These are intelligent adaptations, and they may have served you well.

The difficulty is that a pattern built for one season of life can quietly outlast its usefulness. What once protected you can begin to cost you — leaving you depleted, faintly resentful, and unsure of who you are when you are not being useful to someone else.
Signs you have drifted from yourself
This kind of self-disconnection rarely arrives with a bang. More often it shows up in small, easily-dismissed ways:

items: Struggling to answer simple questions like "what would you like to do?"
Feeling guilty or anxious when you rest or say no.
Automatically prioritising others' comfort over your own, even in small things.
A vague sense of numbness, flatness, or living life at one remove.
Resentment that builds quietly and then surprises you with its force.

body.text: None of these mean you have failed. They are simply signals — information from a self that would like to be included again.
Small ways to begin coming back
Reconnecting does not require a dramatic reinvention. It usually begins with small, low-stakes moments of turning inward and asking, gently, how am I, and what do I want here? A few starting places:

items: Notice your preferences in tiny, everyday choices — which drink, which route, which music — and let them count.
Practise pausing before you say yes, giving yourself a beat to check in with what you actually feel.
Reclaim a small pocket of time that is entirely yours, without justifying it.
Let yourself feel resentment or tiredness without rushing to explain it away — take it as information.
Reconnect with something you used to love before life filled up.

body.text: Expect it to feel awkward at first. Prioritising yourself after years of not doing so can trigger guilt, and that guilt is not a sign you are doing something wrong. It is often just the old pattern protesting the change.
You do not have to do it alone

Some of this work is easier with a steady companion. Counselling can offer a space where your needs are not too much, where you can slow down and get reacquainted with what you feel and want — without having to look after anyone else in the room. If you would like to understand the person you might do this with, you can read a little more [about me and how I work](/about).

Coming back to yourself is not selfish, and it does not mean caring less for the people you love. Often it is the opposite: when you are more in contact with yourself, your care becomes freely given rather than automatically extracted. If any of this resonates, you can read about how we might [work together in individual counselling](/work-with-me/psychological-counselling), and you are welcome to [get in touch](/contact) whenever the time feels right.
